title: Billboard review of the Rainbow Ballroom, Denver, November 1941
summary: Love reads a 1941 Billboard review of Fields' first colored band engagement at the Rainbow, noting instrumentation and soloists, and recalls meeting Fields that day.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: After we saw this write up here, I got so many compliments on that.
This was November 8, 1941, Billboard, and it says: Reviewed at the

Rainbow Ballroom, Denver, Ernie Fields. Fields' engagement here was the first for a colored combination, other than for one-nighters and his week showing was one of the best the ballroom has had in several years. Music (inaudible) in that Fields kept on the swing side as well as the usual boogie. Library is extensive enough to cover both. Rene Hall takes care of the boogie arrangements while Gay Jones, the paleface, has been doing the sweet work. Regular instrumentation is four reeds, five brass, split three trumpets and two trombones and four rhythm. Guitar player doubles on trombone,--that would be Rene Hall--and Fields also takes a turn at the sliphorn to fill to seven brass. Leon Thomas is a standout at the piano and also doubles on the electric violin for sweet work. Bugda (phonetic spelling)--which was Richard Bugda,--on tenor and Luther West, alto, take the reed leads. Hall is often featured with his guitar work. A swing combo of guitar and violin, clarinet and bass paces the outfit in

that type of tune. Vocal department is handled by Stella Edmonson--Estelle Edmonson--and Melvin Moore. Both are good soloists, former doing jive work while Moore works with the ballads. Different from the good many colored fronters, Fields works for the crowd, using a goodly amount of (inaudible).

That's when I met you, November 8, 1941. My wife and I were on our honeymoon, we were working in Boulder, we met you in front of the hotel, you were getting in your flexible, (inaudible). You, Melvin Moore and Cornbread--tenor sax--
Singer; that was Harold Singer; wasn't it?
